summary: A 1970 note on an official protocol mechanism, by Steve Crocker. It concerns how protocols would be formally put forward within the group.

eli5.summary: This note is about how the group would officially announce a finished set of rules.

subtitle: Steve Crocker sets out a six-step process for proposing, reviewing and approving the official Host-Host protocol.

tldr.problem: The network community needed agreed rules for establishing and changing an official Host-Host protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Proposals are issued as NWG/RFCs, the community comments before a cutoff date, and the ARPA office approves or rejects the whole proposal.
tldr.outcome: The note records decisions made by five people at the Spring Joint Computer Conference and promises the first official protocol that month.

facts.label: Place
facts.value: Spring Joint Computer Conference, Atlantic City

today: RFC 53 is a 1970 process note, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text does not say how long the process stayed in use.

sections.title: Where the Rules Came From
sections.content:
RFC 53, written by S. Crocker of UCLA and dated 9 June 70, reports a discussion held during the Spring Joint Computer Conference in Atlantic City. Larry Roberts, Barry Wessler, Cordell Green, Jon Postel and Crocker talked about rules for establishing and modifying an official Host-Host protocol.

The note lists six decisions. It describes a process, not a protocol.
sections.eli5: Some grown-ups met and agreed on how the group would make official rules.

sections.title: The Six Decisions
sections.content:
First, a new set of documents will specify the official Host-Host protocol, and when appropriate these will be kept at the Network Information Center on SRI's computer. Crocker will distribute proposals for the first version and every later change as NWG/RFCs, formed from suggestions by any interested parties.

After a proposal is issued, networkers are asked to respond with approval, criticism and so on, and each protocol carries a cutoff date.

  • If substantial criticism arrives by the cutoff, the process stops and the official protocol does not change.
  • If the proposal is substantially accepted, it goes with its minor revisions to the ARPA office, where Barry Wessler or his successor approves or disapproves the whole proposal by letter to Crocker.
  • After approval, Crocker sends out the new protocol.
sections.eli5: Someone writes an idea, everyone has until a deadline to say what they think, and then one person decides yes or no for the whole idea.

sections.title: What Came Next
sections.content: The note ends by saying that the first version of an official protocol will be proferred that month. It does not name that protocol or say what it contains.
sections.eli5: The note says the first official rulebook is coming soon.
